# Discussion

Bat activity is shaped by seasonal phenology and multiple nightly environmental drivers that covary in the field. We used a directed acyclic graph to formalize hypothesized relationships among these drivers and to distinguish the seasonal and conditional environmental quantities represented by our models [@pearl2009]. We then stratified activity by characteristic echolocation frequency to test mechanistic predictions arising from frequency-dependent atmospheric attenuation [@lawrence1982]. This framework revealed substantial environmental and phenological structure that would have been difficult to interpret from a single community-level additive model.

## Seasonal phenology and nightly environmental conditions

The aggregate analysis distinguished the seasonal pattern observed under naturally changing environmental conditions from the seasonal structure remaining after nightly temperature, relative humidity, and lunar phase were held constant. **\[UPDATE AFTER FINAL SEASONAL FIGURE: describe the final total and conditional seasonal curves, including whether the previously identified summer peak versus spring/autumn residual pattern persists under the negative-binomial factor-smooth models.\]**

An important refinement of the current analysis is that seasonal phenology was allowed to vary among sites. Although the eight sites were geographically close, their seasonal activity trajectories differed substantially in timing and magnitude. These differences need not imply distinct regional seasons. Local habitat, elevation, roost proximity, species composition, resource availability, and the timing of local site use can all produce different seasonal activity trajectories within the same regional climatic regime. Representing those differences explicitly greatly reduced the persistent residual autocorrelation present in simpler models, suggesting that much of what initially appeared to be a time-series problem was unmodeled ecological heterogeneity in seasonal phenology.

If the spring-and-autumn residual seasonal structure identified in the previous analysis persists, the frequency-stratified results will help determine its biological basis. The previous models suggested that spring and autumn activity windows were concentrated in low- and mid-frequency groups containing migratory *Lasiurus*, *Lasionycteris*, and *Tadarida*, whereas high-frequency *Myotis* showed steadier activity through the season, an interpretation consistent with documented migratory phenology in western North American bats [@cryan2003; @weller2016] and with evidence that temperature and night length jointly structure bat activity [@lilley2026]. **\[Retain or revise this interpretation after the final frequency-group seasonal curves are examined.\]**

## Humidity and echolocation frequency

The central mechanistic prediction of this study is that humidity sensitivity should vary with characteristic echolocation frequency because atmospheric absorption of ultrasound is frequency dependent [@griffin1971; @lawrence1982]. The previous frequency-stratified models produced the predicted qualitative ordering: little humidity response in the low-frequency group, a threshold-like decline at high humidity in the mid-frequency group, and a broader monotonic decline in the high-frequency group. **\[UPDATE WITH FINAL FREQUENCY-GROUP MODELS: confirm whether these three response shapes persist and replace this sentence with quantitative posterior predictions.\]**

If supported by the final models, this correspondence would extend a longstanding physical hypothesis about atmospheric attenuation from measurements of call transmission and individual detection distance to community-level activity patterns. At low ultrasonic frequencies, humidity should have relatively little influence on sound transmission; at intermediate frequencies, sensitivity increases over part of the humidity gradient; and at high frequencies, attenuation is more strongly humidity-dependent across a broader range [@griffin1971; @lawrence1982]. Experimental and modeling studies have shown that atmospheric conditions can alter prey-detection distance and that bats may not fully compensate for increased attenuation by changing call structure [@deframond2023; @luo2014]. A frequency-ordered field response would therefore provide a mechanistically interpretable link between atmospheric physics and community-level activity.

The causal structure is important for this interpretation. Humidity varies seasonally and is associated with temperature, so an unadjusted humidity relationship could reflect weather or seasonal phenology rather than acoustic attenuation. Our conditional models estimate humidity responses while accounting for day of year, temperature, lunar phase, and local seasonal phenology. This does not prove that attenuation alone causes the observed activity response, but it makes the frequency-dependent attenuation hypothesis more directly testable than a marginal community-level comparison.

## Temperature and thermal niches

Temperature remained an important conditional correlate of aggregate bat activity after accounting for seasonal phenology, humidity, and lunar phase. This is consistent with the broad literature showing increased bat activity on warmer nights across temperate systems [@bender2015; @jorge2021; @mas2022; @russoPetrick2023; @wolbert2014]. Temperature can influence bats through several pathways, including thermoregulatory costs, prey availability, and the duration or profitability of nightly foraging.

The previous frequency-group models suggested substantial heterogeneity in temperature responses: a modest response in low-frequency bats, a strong positive response in the mid-frequency group, and an unusual cool-temperature peak in the high-frequency group. **\[UPDATE AFTER FINAL FREQUENCY-GROUP FITS. Do not retain the old cold-tolerance interpretation unless the pattern persists under the corrected sampling frame and site-specific seasonal model.\]** If a cool-temperature response remains evident, it should be evaluated against the distribution of observations and site contributions before being interpreted as thermal niche differentiation. The earlier interpretation invoked cold tolerance in small-bodied *Myotis* [@audet1996; @lausen2003; @tuttle1974], but the revised model now accounts much more explicitly for local seasonal site use, which may alter that conclusion.

More generally, frequency groups are not pure physiological guilds: they combine species that differ in body size, migratory strategy, roosting ecology, and foraging habitat. Differences among frequency-group temperature curves therefore should be interpreted as assemblage-level ecological responses rather than effects of call frequency itself. This distinction is especially important because call frequency provides a direct mechanistic prediction for humidity attenuation but only an indirect grouping of species with respect to thermal physiology.

## Lunar phase

Lunar phase was a weaker environmental correlate than temperature and relative humidity in the aggregate model. The published literature reports responses ranging from lunar phobia to little detectable effect, particularly among temperate insectivorous bats [@morrison1978; @hecker1999; @karlsson2002; @milne2005; @saldanavazquez2013]. Some of this inconsistency may arise because lunar phase is analyzed without adequate representation of seasonal and weather covariation.

**\[UPDATE AFTER FINAL AGGREGATE AND FREQUENCY-GROUP LUNAR PREDICTIONS.\]** The previous models suggested modestly higher activity toward the full moon across frequency groups. We should retain that biological interpretation only if the predicted response remains meaningful under the final negative-binomial, site-specific seasonal models. Regardless of direction, the revised analysis allows the lunar response to be interpreted conditional on seasonal phenology and nightly weather rather than as an unadjusted lunar association.

## Model adequacy and temporal structure

The model-development process also provides an important methodological lesson for long-duration passive acoustic studies. Nights on which a detector failed are not ecological zeroes. Treating equipment failure as absence of bat activity would artificially add zero counts and could distort both seasonal trajectories and environmental relationships. After reconstructing detector effort, we excluded site-nights without evidence that the acoustic detector operated and retained zeroes only for sampled nights with no detected activity.

Likewise, residual temporal autocorrelation did not disappear simply by replacing a Poisson likelihood with a negative-binomial likelihood. Overdispersion and temporal structure represented different deficiencies. The major reduction in persistent autocorrelation occurred when we allowed seasonal phenology to vary among sites. In the final aggregate environmental model, residual correlation declined rapidly over the first several calendar-day lags and was approximately zero by lag four. This suggests that the principal long-range dependence in the simpler models arose from unmodeled local seasonal trajectories rather than from a single autoregressive process shared across sites.

Some short-lag dependence remained, particularly in the season-only model. We did not add an autoregressive term solely to force residual correlations toward zero because the remaining dependence was short-lived, the major ecological structure had been represented explicitly, and posterior predictive checks indicated adequate recovery of the response features relevant to our estimands. In ecological systems, an increasingly complex model is not necessarily a more useful model; adequacy depends on whether the model represents the biological and sampling processes needed for the scientific questions.

## Ecological implications

Bat communities should not be expected to respond uniformly to changing environmental conditions. Seasonal timing, thermal physiology, foraging ecology, and echolocation acoustics provide different pathways through which environmental change can alter activity. If the predicted frequency-dependent humidity responses persist in the final models, increasing humidity or altered precipitation regimes could impose stronger acoustic constraints on high-frequency than low-frequency foragers. Changes in temperature may simultaneously alter prey availability, thermoregulatory costs, and seasonal activity windows. Migratory and resident components of the assemblage may therefore respond differently even within a geographically compact study area.

More broadly, these analyses illustrate the value of making the estimand and causal assumptions explicit before interpreting coefficients from multivariable ecological models. Environmental predictors in field studies rarely vary independently. A model that includes every available predictor may estimate useful conditional associations, but those associations are not automatically equivalent to total ecological effects. Combining causal reasoning with flexible nonlinear models and explicit representation of sampling and local phenology can make the biological interpretation of passive-monitoring data more defensible.

**\[FINAL PARAGRAPH TO UPDATE AFTER FREQUENCY MODELS.\]** Once the final frequency-group models are accepted, end with the strongest supported synthesis: whether the study demonstrates frequency-dependent humidity sensitivity, thermal differentiation among assemblage components, and/or a revised understanding of seasonal phenology. Avoid making the causal language stronger than the DAG and observational design support.
